claims.source: Substantially fewer genes were negatively regulated in these merged groups, with only 14 significantly down-regulated genes found in Six1+Eya1m, 11 in Six1m and 13 in Eya1m (Supplementary file 3, Tables 4–6), re-enforcing the notion that together, Six1 and Eya1 act primarily as transcriptional activators (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is a direct report of the merged RNA-Seq data analysis results.

claims.claim: Together, Six1 and Eya1 act primarily as transcriptional activators.
claims.source: Substantially fewer genes were negatively regulated in these merged groups, with only 14 significantly down-regulated genes found in Six1+Eya1m, 11 in Six1m and 13 in Eya1m (Supplementary file 3, Tables 4–6), re-enforcing the notion that together, Six1 and Eya1 act primarily as transcriptional activators (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that more genes are up-regulated than down-regulated.

claims.claim: Transcription factors and protein binding together accounted for the largest fraction of up-regulated genes (53% in total) in the Six1+Eya1m merged data set.
claims.source: Presumptive direct targets that were significantly up-regulated in our merged data set (Six1+Eya1m) were analysed using Panther (Mi et al., 2013) to examine the representation of genes grouped by molecular function (Figure 2D). Transcription factors and protein binding together accounted for the largest fraction of up-regulated genes (53% in total), followed by enzymes (30%) and transporter molecules (13%), suggesting a developmental function of many of the genes up-regulated by either Six1 or Eya1.
claims.evidence: This is based on Panther analysis of the merged RNA-Seq data, as shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Genes directly up-regulated by Six1, Eya1 or Six1+Eya1 were highly enriched for terms associated with sense organ development, inner-ear development, mechanoreceptor differentiation, eye morphogenesis, neurogenesis and axon guidance.
claims.source: GSEA was then conducted using DAVID (Huang et al., 2009) on the sets of significantly up- or down-regulated genes in our merged data sets, as well as in various combinations of subsets of differentially expressed genes from our individual treatment groups (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1). This analysis showed that genes directly up-regulated by Six1, Eya1 or Six1+Eya1 were highly enriched for terms associated with sense organ development, inner-ear development, mechanoreceptor differentiation, eye morphogenesis, neurogenesis and axon guidance consistent with their synergistic role in sensory development (Grocott et al., 2012; Schlosser, 2010) and neurogenesis (Maier et al., 2014; Schlosser and Northcutt, 2000).
claims.evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis of the merged RNA-Seq data, as shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Genes encoding cell cycle regulators (CyclinD, RGCC), cell surface receptors and adhesion molecules (e.g. CXCR7, EDAR, Protocadherin11, Claudin3, Fzd1, Fzd4,), secreted proteins (e.g. FGF3, FGF19, Dkk1, Neurotrophin3) and cytoskeletal regulators (e.g. RhoV, Espin) with known or potential roles in placode development were also up-regulated.
claims.source: Apart from genes encoding transcription factors involved in sensory development (see below), genes encoding cell cycle regulators (CyclinD, RGCC), cell surface receptors and adhesion molecules (e.g. CXCR7, EDAR, Protocadherin11, Claudin3, Fzd1, Fzd4,), secreted proteins (e.g. FGF3, FGF19, Dkk1, Neurotrophin3) and cytoskeletal regulators (e.g. RhoV, Espin) with known or potential roles in placode development were also up-regulated.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Hox genes (specifically of the Antennapedia-type) were extremely enriched in the Eya1-specific subset of up-regulated genes.
claims.source: A particularly interesting finding was the extreme enrichment of Hox genes (specifically of the Antennapedia-type) in the Eya1-specific subset of up-regulated genes (Figure 3F), suggesting that Eya1 may play a previously un-identified role in regulating Hox gene expression independently of Six1.
claims.evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis of the RNA-Seq data, as shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Eya1 may play a previously un-identified role in regulating Hox gene expression independently of Six1.
claims.source: A particularly interesting finding was the extreme enrichment of Hox genes (specifically of the Antennapedia-type) in the Eya1-specific subset of up-regulated genes (Figure 3F), suggesting that Eya1 may play a previously un-identified role in regulating Hox gene expression independently of Six1.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the GSEA analysis showing enrichment of Hox genes in Eya1-specific targets.

claims.claim: A list of well-supported target genes was generated containing all genes with at least a two-fold up-regulation in at least two of the three treatment groups.
claims.source: To verify our RNA-Seq data, we selected a number of target genes for further characterisation and, in order to gain insight into the GRN downstream of Six1 and Eya1, we restricted candidates to transcription factors or co-factors up-regulated by Six1 or Eya1. First, we generated a list of well-supported target genes containing all genes with at least a two-fold up-regulation in at least two of our three treatment groups (Table 1).
claims.evidence: This describes the criteria used to select genes for further analysis.

claims.claim: From the 228 genes in the well-supported target gene list, 30 transcription factors or co-factors were selected for further analysis.
claims.source: From the 228 genes in this list we selected all 30 transcription factors or co-factors for further analysis.
claims.evidence: This describes the selection of genes for further analysis.

claims.claim: Sox3 and Ngn1 were included in the analysis because previous studies have implicated these genes in the regulation of placodal neurogenesis downstream of Six1 and Eya1.
claims.source: We additionally included Sox3 and Ngn1 - which were found to be slightly below our threshold of twofold up-regulation in at least two treatment groups - because previous studies have implicated these genes in the regulation of placodal neurogenesis downstream of Six1 and Eya1 (Ma et al., 1996, 1998; Schlosser et al., 2008; Ahmed et al., 2012b) (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Ma et al., 1996, 1998; Schlosser et al., 2008; Ahmed et al., 2012b.

claims.claim: 19/30 (63.3%) of the transcriptional regulators selected for analysis were expressed in PPE or placodal derivatives.
claims.source: We found 19/30 (63.3% ) of these transcriptional regulators to be expressed in PPE or placodal derivatives, while 11/30 (Sox17, MyoD1, Sox1, Ets2a, Mafa, Emx1.2, Lhx5, Pou3f2b, Tbx6, Tbx15, Sim1) were not expressed in either the PPE or any placodal derivatives.
claims.evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization analysis of the selected genes.

claims.claim: 11/30 transcriptional regulators (Sox17, MyoD1, Sox1, Ets2a, Mafa, Emx1.2, Lhx5, Pou3f2b, Tbx6, Tbx15, Sim1) were not expressed in either the PPE or any placodal derivatives.
claims.source: We found 19/30 (63.3% ) of these transcriptional regulators to be expressed in PPE or placodal derivatives, while 11/30 (Sox17, MyoD1, Sox1, Ets2a, Mafa, Emx1.2, Lhx5, Pou3f2b, Tbx6, Tbx15, Sim1) were not expressed in either the PPE or any placodal derivatives.
claims.evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization analysis of the selected genes.

claims.claim: Many of the genes not expressed in the PPE or placodal derivatives were expressed in the adjacent neural folds or other tissues.
claims.source: However, many of the genes in the latter group were expressed in the adjacent neural folds or other tissues. Thus, it is possible that such genes may be direct targets of Six1 or Eya1 in domains surrounding the PPE, likely to have been included in our screen as a result of non-PPE contamination during dissection.
claims.evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization analysis and is an inference about the reason for their inclusion in the screen.

claims.claim: 79% (15/19) of the transcriptional regulators expressed in the PPE or placodal derivatives were statistically supported in the analyses of merged datasets.
claims.source: Of the transcriptional regulators identified in our list of well-supported targets and expressed in the PPE or placodal derivatives 79% (15/19) were statistically supported in the analyses of merged datasets (Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the merged RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Selected genes were independently verified as being direct targets of either Six1 (Isl2) or of both Six1 and Eya1 (all other targets; Sox3 not analysed) in the PPE by qPCR.
claims.source: Selected genes were independently verified as being direct targets of either Six1 (Isl2) or of both Six1 and Eya1 (all other targets; Sox3 not analysed) in the PPE by qPCR, and the results were broadly consistent with the RNA-Seq data (Figure 4U and V).
claims.evidence: This is based on qPCR validation experiments, as shown in Figure 4U and V.

claims.claim: Knockdown of either Six1 or Eya1 significantly reduced the expression of all direct target genes in PPE or placodes.
claims.source: Compared to injection with a control MO (Eya1-mmMO with 5 mismatches relative to Eya1-MO2), knockdown of either Six1 or Eya1 significantly reduced the expression of all direct target genes in PPE or placodes, demonstrating that both Six1 and Eya1 are required for their expression (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Table 3).
claims.evidence: This is based on loss-of-function experiments using morpholinos, as shown in Figure 5 and Table 3.

claims.claim: Expression patterns of all target genes after overexpression of a dominant-negative version of Six1 (Six1-EnR) were highly similar to those seen after MO-knockdown of either Six1 or Eya1.
claims.source: To control for off-target effects associated with MO use, target gene expression was also analysed after overexpression of a dominant-negative version of Six1 (Six1-EnR; Brugmann et al., 2004). Expression patterns of all target genes were highly similar to those seen after MO-knockdown of either Six1 or Eya1, suggesting that the observed reductions in expression were caused by Six1 or Eya1 knockdown as opposed to being an artefact of MO use (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on experiments using a dominant-negative construct, as shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Six1 and Eya1 are essential direct upstream regulators of multiple genes encoding transcription factors that promote neuro- and sensorigenesis in the PPE and placodes.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings show that Six1 and Eya1 are essential direct upstream regulators of multiple genes encoding transcription factors that promote neuro- and sensorigenesis in the PPE and placodes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments.

claims.claim: Injection of Six1-GR or Eya1-GR resulted in up-regulation of direct targets in a minority of cases.
claims.source: Surprisingly, although injection of Six1-GR or Eya1-GR resulted in up-regulation of direct targets in a minority of cases (Table 3; Figures 6 and 7), the dominant observed phenotype was down-regulation of target gene expression in the PPE or placodes (Table 3; Figures 8 and 9).
claims.evidence: This is based on gain-of-function experiments using hormone-inducible constructs, as shown in Table 3 and Figures 6-9.

claims.claim: The dominant observed phenotype after injection of Six1-GR or Eya1-GR was down-regulation of target gene expression in the PPE or placodes.
claims.source: Surprisingly, although injection of Six1-GR or Eya1-GR resulted in up-regulation of direct targets in a minority of cases (Table 3; Figures 6 and 7), the dominant observed phenotype was down-regulation of target gene expression in the PPE or placodes (Table 3; Figures 8 and 9).
claims.evidence: This is based on gain-of-function experiments using hormone-inducible constructs, as shown in Table 3 and Figures 8 and 9.

claims.claim: Six1 and Eya1 additionally affect expression of many of their direct target genes in indirect and partly opposing ways.
claims.source: Considering that here, unlike in the initial RNA-Seq screen and qPCR experiments, CHX was not used to block protein synthesis, these results indicate that Six1 and Eya1 additionally affect expression of many of their direct target genes in indirect and partly opposing ways.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that gain-of-function experiments without CHX show different results than the initial screen with CHX.

claims.claim: Overexpression of GR-fusion constructs followed by DEX-induced nuclear translocation in the presence of protein synthesis inhibitors has been previously used successfully to screen for direct target genes of transcription factors or cofactors in Xenopus.
claims.source: Overexpression of GR-fusion constructs followed by DEX-induced nuclear translocation in the presence of protein synthesis inhibitors has been previously used successfully to screen for direct target genes of transcription factors or cofactors in Xenopus (Kolm and Sive, 1995; Taverner et al., 2005; Seo et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Kolm and Sive, 1995; Taverner et al., 2005; Seo et al., 2007.

claims.claim: This strategy recovers the majority of direct Six1 target genes known from previous studies, indicating its reliability.
claims.source: Here, we combine this approach with high-throughput sequencing of tissue-specific RNA to identify several hundred novel presumptive direct target genes of Six1 and Eya1 in the PPE. We show that this strategy indeed recovers the majority of direct Six1 target genes known from previous studies, indicating its reliability.
claims.evidence: This is based on the validation of the RNA-Seq approach by comparing results to known targets.

claims.claim: In situ and qPCR analyses of target genes predicted from the RNA-Seq screen provided independent verification of selected target genes suggesting a low false discovery rate.
claims.source: Our in situ and qPCR analyses of target genes predicted from the RNA-Seq screen also provided independent verification of selected target genes suggesting a low false discovery rate.
claims.evidence: This is based on the validation experiments using in situ hybridization and qPCR.

claims.claim: The expression of all genes selected for detailed analysis proved to be dependent on Six1 and Eya1 in the PPE.
claims.source: Moreover, the expression of all genes selected for detailed analysis proved to be dependent on Six1 and Eya1 in the PPE, indicating that many genes our screen predicted as Six1/Eya1 targets are also functionally dependent on these upstream regulators in the PPE.
claims.evidence: This is based on the loss-of-function experiments.

claims.claim: A comparison of the data set with recently identified direct target genes of sine oculis, the Six1 orthologue in the developing eye of Drosophila, reveals that homologues to six out of the 12 sine oculis target genes identified with high confidence are differentially expressed in the Sixi or Six1+Eya1i (and often also in Eya1i) treatment groups.
claims.source: A comparison of our data set with recently identified direct target genes of sine oculis, the Six1 orthologue in the developing eye of Drosophila (Jusiak et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2016) also reveals that homologues to six out of the 12 sine oculis target genes identified with high confidence in Jin et al. (2016) are differentially expressed in our Sixi or Six1+Eya1i (and often also in Eya1i) treatment groups, viz. Six1 and Six2; Eya4; Shh; various matrix metalloproteases (e.g. MMP9); Ets2; and Frizzled1 and Frizzled4.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of the RNA-Seq data with published data from Drosophila.

claims.claim: A relatively high proportion of Six1 target genes may be evolutionarily conserved.
claims.source: This suggests that a relatively high proportion of Six1 target genes may be evolutionarily conserved.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison with Drosophila data.

claims.claim: Without blocking protein synthesis it is not possible to reliably identify direct target genes, presumably due to the existence of indirect interactions with such targets.
claims.source: Our finding that many of the presumptive direct target genes of Six1 or Eya1 are not up-regulated in the absence of CHX indicates that without blocking protein synthesis it is not possible to reliably identify direct target genes, presumably due to the existence of indirect interactions with such targets.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that gain-of-function experiments without CHX show different results than the initial screen with CHX.

claims.claim: The findings differ substantially from the study of Yan et al. (2015), which analysed differentially expressed genes in Xenopus animal cap explants after overexpression of Six1 without first blocking protein synthesis.
claims.source: We believe that this is one of the reasons why our findings differ substantially from the study of Yan et al. (2015), which analysed differentially expressed genes in Xenopus animal cap explants after overexpression of Six1 without first blocking protein synthesis. None of the transcription factors in our prioritised list was identified in the study by Yan et al. (2015); and we found none of the transcription factors differentially expressed in their study.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of the current study with a previous study by Yan et al. (2015).

claims.claim: A second likely reason for the discrepancy between the results presented here and in Yan et al. (2015) is that this study specifically analysed PPE tissue while Yan et al. (2015) analysed target genes in animal cap tissue.
claims.source: A second likely reason for the discrepancy between the results presented here and in Yan et al. (2015) is that, while we specifically analysed PPE tissue (presumably containing tissue-specific cofactors required for the activation or repression of Six1 and Eya1 target genes specific for the developing placodes), they analysed target genes in animal cap tissue, known to be composed of pluripotent cells.
claims.evidence: This is an inference about the reason for the discrepancy with the Yan et al. (2015) study.

claims.claim: Previous studies have shown that Six1 and Eya1 are essential for both the establishment of the PPE as well as for the subsequent development of placode-derived sense organs.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that Six1 and Eya1 are essential for both the establishment of the PPE (Brugmann et al., 2004; Christophorou et al., 2009), as well as for the subsequent development of placode-derived sense organs (Xu et al., 1999; Laclef et al., 2003; Zheng et al., 2003; Brugmann et al., 2004; Zou et al., 2004; Kozlowski et al., 2005; Schlosser et al., 2008; Ahmed et al., 2012b, 2012a) but the mechanisms through which they act are poorly understood.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claims.claim: The continued expression of both Six1 and Eya1 in almost all placodes developing from the PPE, combined with the observed deficiencies in derivatives from most placodes after loss-of-function of either Six1 or Eya1, indicates that they play a role in generic aspects of placode development shared by all placodes.
claims.source: The continued expression of both genes in almost all placodes developing from the PPE (Schlosser and Ahrens, 2004), combined with the observed deficiencies in derivatives from most placodes after loss-of-function of either Six1 or Eya1, indicates that they play a role in generic aspects of placode development shared by all placodes.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on expression patterns and loss-of-function studies.

claims.claim: Genes revealed as presumptive direct targets of Six1 and Eya1 were highly enriched for GO terms associated with neurogenesis and placode development.
claims.source: Indeed, our data show that genes revealed as presumptive direct targets of Six1 and Eya1 were highly enriched for GO terms associated with neurogenesis and placode development.
claims.evidence: This is based on GSEA analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: The screen confirms previous studies suggesting that Six1 and Eya1 synergistically regulate many genes in the PPE, and that the Six1-Eya1 protein complex predominantly acts by activating transcription.
claims.source: Our screen also confirms previous studies suggesting that Six1 and Eya1 synergistically regulate many genes in the PPE, and that the Six1-Eya1 protein complex predominantly acts by activating transcription (Li et al., 2003; Brugmann et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the RNA-Seq data and citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: There is support for independent action of Six1 and Eya1 in the PPE, possibly in conjunction with other interacting partners.
claims.source: However, we also find support for independent action of Six1 and Eya1 in the PPE, possibly in conjunction with other interacting partners (Brugmann et al., 2004; Ahmed et al., 2012a).
claims.evidence: This is based on the RNA-Seq data showing genes regulated by Six1 or Eya1 alone, and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: It has previously been suggested that a generic role of Six1 and Eya1 for all placodes could be implemented in two possible ways: (1) By the direct contribution to the activation of genes regulating developmental processes shared between different placodes such as proliferation, morphogenetic movements and neuronal or sensory cytodifferentiation; or (2) by direct contribution to the activation of genes defining the identity of different individual placodes within the PPE.
claims.source: It has previously been suggested (Schlosser, 2006) that a generic role of Six1 and Eya1 for all placodes could be implemented in two possible ways: (1) By the direct contribution to the activation of genes regulating developmental processes shared between different placodes such as proliferation, morphogenetic movements and neuronal or sensory cytodifferentiation; or (2) by direct contribution to the activation of genes defining the identity of different individual placodes within the PPE.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Schlosser, 2006.

claims.claim: The data strongly suggest that Six1 and Eya1 act predominantly in the first rather than in the second mode.
claims.source: Our data strongly suggest that Six1 and Eya1 act predominantly in the first rather than in the second mode.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the types of genes identified as targets in the RNA-Seq screen.

claims.claim: Only a few genes encoding transcription factors implicated in conferring identity to individual placodes were recovered as targets of Six1 or Eya1, e.g. Gbx2 (FC 1.7 in Six1+Eya1i) and FoxI4 (FC 1.09 in Six1i).
claims.source: A large number of transcription factor encoding genes, including several Pax, Pitx, ANF and FoxI genes, have been implicated in conferring identity to individual placodes, or groups of placodes, within the PPE (reviewed in Schlosser, 2006, 2010; Grocott et al., 2012; Saint-Jeannet and Moody, 2014) however only a few of these genes were recovered as targets of Six1 or Eya1, e.g. Gbx2 (FC 1.7 in Six1+Eya1i) and FoxI4 (FC 1.09 in Six1i).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: A large number of genes encoding transcription factors with roles in neuronal/sensory cytodifferentiation but also other proteins with likely roles for the maintenance of proliferating progenitors, the regulation of cell adhesion and morphogenetic movements and cytodifferentiation were found.
claims.source: In contrast, we found a large number of genes encoding transcription factors with roles in neuronal/sensory cytodifferentiation but also other proteins with likely roles for the maintenance of proliferating progenitors (e.g. Cyclin D, RGCC), the regulation of cell adhesion and morphogenetic movements (e.g. EDAR, CXCR7, Protocadherin11, RhoV, Claudin3) and cytodifferentiation (e.g. Espin, Neurotrophin3).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Six1 and Eya1 act as both master genes and micro-managers, acting upstream of a GRN co-ordinating cell differentiation in the PPE as well as directly activating terminal differentiation gene batteries.
claims.source: This suggests that, similar to Hox or Pax genes, Six1 and Eya1 act as both master genes and micro-managers (Akam, 1998; Thompson and Ziman, 2011; Rezsohazy et al., 2015), acting upstream of a GRN co-ordinating cell differentiation in the PPE as well as directly activating terminal differentiation gene batteries.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the types of genes identified as targets and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: Six1 and Eya1 have previously been shown to promote a proliferative progenitor state at high doses but neuronal and sensory differentiation at lower doses.
claims.source: Considering that Six1 and Eya1 have previously been shown to promote a proliferative progenitor state at high doses but neuronal and sensory differentiation at lower doses (Schlosser et al., 2008), it is particularly interesting that we identified presumptive direct target genes encoding transcription factors previously implicated in progenitor maintenance (Sox2, Sox3, Hes8, Hes9) and differentiation (Ngn1, Atoh1, POU4f1, Gfi1a, Isl2, Tlx1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Schlosser et al., 2008.

claims.claim: Presumptive direct target genes encoding transcription factors previously implicated in progenitor maintenance (Sox2, Sox3, Hes8, Hes9) and differentiation (Ngn1, Atoh1, POU4f1, Gfi1a, Isl2, Tlx1) were identified.
claims.source: Considering that Six1 and Eya1 have previously been shown to promote a proliferative progenitor state at high doses but neuronal and sensory differentiation at lower doses (Schlosser et al., 2008), it is particularly interesting that we identified presumptive direct target genes encoding transcription factors previously implicated in progenitor maintenance (Sox2, Sox3, Hes8, Hes9) and differentiation (Ngn1, Atoh1, POU4f1, Gfi1a, Isl2, Tlx1).
claims.evidence: This is based on the RNA-Seq data.

claims.claim: Both Hes (Hes8, Hes9) and SoxB1 (Sox2, Sox3) proteins are known to keep progenitor cells in an undifferentiated state, and must be down-regulated for neuronal differentiation to proceed.
claims.source: Both Hes (Hes8, Hes9) and SoxB1 (Sox2, Sox3) proteins are known to keep progenitor cells in an undifferentiated state, and must be down-regulated for neuronal differentiation to proceed.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge in developmental biology.

claims.claim: Sox2 and Sox3 play multiple roles including activity as pioneer factors, which open up chromatin for transcription.
claims.source: While Sox2 and Sox3 play multiple roles including activity as pioneer factors, which open up chromatin for transcription (Bylund et al., 2003; Graham et al., 2003; Pevny and Placzek, 2005; Bergsland et al., 2011), Hes proteins generally repress neuronal/sensory determination genes such as Ngn1 or Atoh1 as effectors of Notch signalling (Kobayashi and Kageyama, 2014; Su et al., 2015; Abdolazimi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Bylund et al., 2003; Graham et al., 2003; Pevny and Placzek, 2005; Bergsland et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Hes proteins generally repress neuronal/sensory determination genes such as Ngn1 or Atoh1 as effectors of Notch signalling.
claims.source: While Sox2 and Sox3 play multiple roles including activity as pioneer factors, which open up chromatin for transcription (Bylund et al., 2003; Graham et al., 2003; Pevny and Placzek, 2005; Bergsland et al., 2011), Hes proteins generally repress neuronal/sensory determination genes such as Ngn1 or Atoh1 as effectors of Notch signalling (Kobayashi and Kageyama, 2014; Su et al., 2015; Abdolazimi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Kobayashi and Kageyama, 2014; Su et al., 2015; Abdolazimi et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Ngn1 and Atoh1 are known to act as proneural factors that initiate differentiation of sensory neurons and hair cells, respectively.
claims.source: Conversely, Ngn1 and Atoh1 are known to act as proneural factors that initiate differentiation of sensory neurons and hair cells, respectively (Ma et al., 1996, 1998; Bermingham et al., 1999; Millimaki et al., 2007), whereas POU4f1 (previously known as Brn3a), Gfi1a, Isl2 and Tlx1 act further downstream in differentiation of sensory neurons (Patterson and Krieg, 1999; Wallis et al., 2003; Cheng et al., 2004; Eng et al., 2004; Lanier et al., 2009; Dykes et al., 2011), and Gfi1a and the related POU domain factor POU4f3 (or Brn3c) are required for hair cell maintenance and survival (Xiang et al., 1998; Wallis et al., 2003).

claims.source: Conversely, Ngn1 and Atoh1 are known to act as proneural factors that initiate differentiation of sensory neurons and hair cells, respectively (Ma et al., 1996, 1998; Bermingham et al., 1999; Millimaki et al., 2007), whereas POU4f1 (previously known as Brn3a), Gfi1a, Isl2 and Tlx1 act further downstream in differentiation of sensory neurons (Patterson and Krieg, 1999; Wallis et al., 2003; Cheng et al., 2004; Eng et al., 2004; Lanier et al., 2009; Dykes et al., 2011), and Gfi1a and the related POU domain factor POU4f3 (or Brn3c) are required for hair cell maintenance and survival (Xiang et al., 1998; Wallis et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Patterson and Krieg, 1999; Wallis et al., 2003; Cheng et al., 2004; Eng et al., 2004; Lanier et al., 2009; Dykes et al., 2011.

claims.source: Conversely, Ngn1 and Atoh1 are known to act as proneural factors that initiate differentiation of sensory neurons and hair cells, respectively (Ma et al., 1996, 1998; Bermingham et al., 1999; Millimaki et al., 2007), whereas POU4f1 (previously known as Brn3a), Gfi1a, Isl2 and Tlx1 act further downstream in differentiation of sensory neurons (Patterson and Krieg, 1999; Wallis et al., 2003; Cheng et al., 2004; Eng et al., 2004; Lanier et al., 2009; Dykes et al., 2011), and Gfi1a and the related POU domain factor POU4f3 (or Brn3c) are required for hair cell maintenance and survival (Xiang et al., 1998; Wallis et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Xiang et al., 1998; Wallis et al., 2003.

claims.claim: The findings strongly indicate that Six1 and Eya1 directly promote multiple steps during sensory and neuronal development, and act to drive both progenitor maintenance and neuronal differentiation programmes in placodes.
claims.source: Our findings strongly indicate that Six1 and Eya1 directly promote multiple steps during sensory and neuronal development, and act to drive both progenitor maintenance and neuronal differentiation programmes in placodes (summarised in Figure 10), although further functional studies are needed to clarify the mechanism allowing Six1 and Eya1 to maintain the balance between activation of progenitor and differentiation genes.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings and is shown in Figure 10.

claims.evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claims.claim: The analysis of Six1 and Eya1 presumptive direct target genes presented here establishes a GRN regulating the development of cranial vertebrate sensory organs and neurons from the PPE.
claims.source: The analysis of Six1 and Eya1 presumptive direct target genes presented here establishes a GRN regulating the development of cranial vertebrate sensory organs and neurons from the PPE (Figure 10), and identifies a large number of novel putative direct target genes encoding a diverse array of proteins.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the significance of the study and is shown in Figure 10.

claims.claim: The data is an invaluable repository of information for designing further functional studies on early sensory development in vertebrates.

claims.claim: Cell proliferation, morphogenesis and cytodifferentiation are also known to be affected in human patients in which Six1 and Eya1 are dysregulated, leading to sensory deficits after Six1 or Eya1 loss of function mutations or enhanced tumour progression after Six1 or Eya1 up-regulation.
claims.source: Finally, while our study focussed on the role of Six1 and Eya1 during sensory development, cell proliferation, morphogenesis and cytodifferentiation are also known to be affected in human patients in which Six1 and Eya1 are dysregulated, leading to sensory deficits after Six1 or Eya1 loss of function mutations (Kochhar et al., 2007) or enhanced tumour progression after Six1 or Eya1 up-regulation (Blevins et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Kochhar et al., 2007; Blevins et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Many target genes identified in this study may also be misregulated in diseases associated with Six1 and Eya1 dysregulation, potentially opening up exciting new avenues for therapeutic intervention.
claims.source: This suggests that many target genes identified in our study may also be misregulated in these diseases, potentially opening up exciting new avenues for therapeutic intervention.
claims.evidence: This is a speculation about the potential clinical relevance of the findings.

results.result: The pre-placodal ectoderm (PPE) is a common precursor region for all cranial placodes, characterized by Six1 and Eya1 expression, and gives rise to many cranial sensory organs and ganglia.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C6, C7, C11, C12, and C13 are well-established facts in developmental biology, supported by multiple citations throughout the manuscript (e.g., Streit, 2002; Schlosser and Ahrens, 2004). These claims provide essential background knowledge for the study.

results.result: Six1 is a transcription factor and Eya1 is a transcriptional co-activator with phosphatase activity; they form a protein complex that synergistically activates transcription, though both can interact with other partners.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C18 describe the molecular properties of Six1 and Eya1, supported by citations to established literature (Kumar, 2009; Ohto et al., 1999; Li et al., 2013; Brugmann et al., 2004; Ahmed et al., 2012a). This provides necessary context for understanding the experimental approach.

results.result: Loss of Six1 or Eya1 function leads to PPE and placodal defects across multiple model organisms and causes congenital hearing loss in humans; these proteins are core regulators of placode development, promoting proliferation and differentiation of sensory cells and neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 summarize prior work demonstrating the importance of Six1 and Eya1 in placode development, supported by extensive citations to studies in multiple model organisms and human patients (Xu et al., 1999; Kochhar et al., 2007; Zou et al., 2004; Ahmed et al., 2012a). This establishes the rationale for the current study.

results.result: This study presents the first comprehensive screen for presumptive direct target genes of Six1 and Eya1 in developing placodes using RNA-Seq in Xenopus laevis, employing hormone-inducible constructs and protein synthesis inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C30 describe the novelty and experimental approach of the study. The methodology is well-established (supported by citations to Kolm and Sive, 1995; Seo et al., 2007) and the claim of being the first comprehensive screen is supported by the lack of prior similar studies (C25).

results.result: The PPE transcriptome comprises 15,794 transcripts, with RNA processing/splicing and translation elongation/ribosomal proteins highly enriched, suggesting important roles for RNA-binding proteins and high protein turnover.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 describe the baseline PPE transcriptome analysis. The data processing is clearly described (C35-C36), and the GSEA results (C37-C38) are supported by the data and appropriate citations (Simões-Costa et al., 2014; McCabe et al., 2004). The inference about protein turnover (C38) is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: RNA-Seq identified 365 genes up-regulated and 292 down-regulated in Six1i, 508 up-regulated and 218 down-regulated in Eya1i, and 836 up-regulated and 490 down-regulated in Six1+Eya1i treatment groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C44 directly report the RNA-Seq data analysis results, as shown in Figure 2A and B and Supplementary file 2. The numbers are specific and verifiable from the data presented.

results.result: The RNA-Seq approach successfully identified most known Six1 target genes from previous studies, confirming the utility of the method for identifying direct targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 validate the RNA-Seq approach by comparing results to known targets from the literature. The recovery of most known targets (except c-Myc) and the expected co-regulation patterns (C47) support the reliability of the method.

results.result: About half of all differentially expressed genes show evidence of co-regulation by Six1 and Eya1, with more genes up-regulated than down-regulated, though a subset of genes are synergistically down-regulated.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C52 analyze the patterns of gene regulation by Six1 and Eya1. The data are supported by Figure 2A and B and statistical analysis (C50). The inference that Eya1 may not always act as a co-activator (C52) is reasonable based on the observation of down-regulated genes.

results.result: 283 genes are regulated by Six1 independently of Eya1, and 426 genes are regulated by Eya1 independently of Six1, suggesting regulation in conjunction with other co-factors or transcription factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 identify genes regulated independently by Six1 or Eya1, based on analysis of the RNA-Seq data (Figure 2A, B). The inference about other co-factors is reasonable but speculative.

results.result: Merged analysis identified 181 significantly up-regulated genes in Six1+Eya1m, 149 in Six1m, and 112 in Eya1m, with substantially fewer down-regulated genes, reinforcing that Six1 and Eya1 act primarily as transcriptional activators.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C59 report the results of the merged dataset analysis (Supplementary file 3, Tables 1-6). The statistical support (q<0.05) is clearly stated, and the inference about transcriptional activation (C59) is supported by the data and prior literature.

results.result: Transcription factors and protein binding account for 53% of up-regulated genes, and genes are highly enriched for terms associated with sense organ development, neurogenesis, and axon guidance, consistent with roles in sensory development.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 describe the functional analysis of up-regulated genes using Panther and GSEA (Figure 2D, Figure 3). The enrichment results are supported by the data and consistent with known roles of Six1 and Eya1 (citations to Grocott et al., 2012; Schlosser, 2010).

results.result: Hox genes (Antennapedia-type) are extremely enriched in the Eya1-specific subset of up-regulated genes, suggesting Eya1 may regulate Hox gene expression independently of Six1.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 report a novel finding from GSEA analysis (Figure 3F). The enrichment is supported by the data, and the inference about Eya1's role in Hox gene regulation (C64) is reasonable but requires further validation.

results.result: From 228 well-supported target genes, 30 transcription factors/co-factors were selected for analysis; 19/30 (63.3%) were expressed in PPE or placodal derivatives, with 79% (15/19) statistically supported in merged datasets.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C71 describe the selection and validation of target genes for further analysis. The criteria are clearly stated (C65), and the in situ hybridization results (C68-C70) provide independent validation. The statistical support (C71) strengthens the findings.

results.result: Selected genes were independently verified as direct targets of Six1 or Six1 and Eya1 by qPCR, with results broadly consistent with RNA-Seq data.
results.evaluation: Claim C72 describes qPCR validation of selected target genes (Figure 4U and V). The independent verification using a different method strengthens the RNA-Seq findings.

results.result: Knockdown of Six1 or Eya1 significantly reduced expression of all direct target genes in PPE or placodes, and similar results were obtained with a dominant-negative Six1 construct, demonstrating that Six1 and Eya1 are essential upstream regulators.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 describe loss-of-function experiments using morpholinos and a dominant-negative construct (Figure 5, Table 3, Figure 5—figure supplement 2). The use of multiple approaches (morpholinos and dominant-negative) controls for off-target effects and strengthens the conclusion that Six1 and Eya1 are required for target gene expression.

results.result: Gain-of-function experiments without protein synthesis inhibition showed that Six1-GR or Eya1-GR injection resulted in down-regulation of target gene expression in most cases, indicating that Six1 and Eya1 affect target gene expression in indirect and partly opposing ways.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 describe gain-of-function experiments without CHX (Table 3, Figures 6-9). The observation that most target genes are down-regulated without CHX, in contrast to the up-regulation observed with CHX in the initial screen, supports the inference that Six1 and Eya1 have indirect effects on target gene expression (C78).

results.result: The GR-fusion construct approach with protein synthesis inhibition is a reliable method for identifying direct target genes, as demonstrated by recovery of known targets, independent verification by in situ and qPCR, and functional dependence of selected genes on Six1 and Eya1.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C82 validate the overall experimental approach. The method is supported by prior literature (C79), recovery of known targets (C80), independent verification (C81), and functional validation (C82). These multiple lines of evidence support the reliability of the approach.

results.result: Comparison with Drosophila sine oculis target genes reveals that homologues to six out of 12 high-confidence targets are differentially expressed in the current study, suggesting evolutionary conservation of Six1 target genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C84 compare the current results with published Drosophila data (Jusiak et al., 2014; Jin et al., 2016). The overlap of 50% of high-confidence targets supports the inference of evolutionary conservation (C84), though this is based on a small sample size.

results.result: Without blocking protein synthesis, it is not possible to reliably identify direct target genes due to indirect interactions; this explains the discrepancy with the Yan et al. (2015) study, which did not use protein synthesis inhibition and analyzed animal cap tissue instead of PPE.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 explain the importance of protein synthesis inhibition and the differences from the Yan et al. (2015) study. The inference (C85) is supported by the observation that gain-of-function experiments without CHX show different results (C76-C78). The comparison with Yan et al. (C86-C87) is reasonable but relies on the assumption that tissue specificity and protein synthesis inhibition are the main factors explaining the discrepancy.

results.result: Six1 and Eya1 are essential for PPE establishment and placode development, playing a role in generic aspects of placode development; the current study confirms their synergistic action in activating transcription and also finds support for independent action.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C92 summarize prior knowledge (C88) and the current findings (C89-C92). The GSEA results (C90) and the patterns of gene regulation (C91-C92) are supported by the data and consistent with prior literature.

results.result: Six1 and Eya1 act predominantly by directly activating genes regulating developmental processes shared between placodes (proliferation, morphogenesis, differentiation) rather than by activating genes defining individual placode identity; they act as both master genes and micro-managers.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C97 interpret the types of genes identified as targets. The inference that Six1 and Eya1 act predominantly in the first mode (C94) is supported by the observation that few placode identity genes were recovered as targets (C95), while many genes involved in proliferation, morphogenesis, and differentiation were found (C96). The comparison to Hox and Pax genes (C97) is supported by citations.

results.result: Six1 and Eya1 directly promote multiple steps during sensory and neuronal development by activating genes encoding transcription factors involved in both progenitor maintenance (Sox2, Sox3, Hes8, Hes9) and differentiation (Ngn1, Atoh1, POU4f1, Gfi1a, Isl2, Tlx1).
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C106 describe the identification of target genes involved in progenitor maintenance and differentiation. The identification of these genes (C99) is supported by the RNA-Seq data. The known roles of these genes (C100-C105) are supported by extensive citations. The inference that Six1 and Eya1 directly promote multiple steps (C106) is supported by the data, though the mechanism for balancing progenitor maintenance and differentiation is acknowledged as requiring further study.

results.result: Direct binding of Six1 to regulatory regions of targets should be confirmed by ChIP-Seq.
results.evaluation: Claim C107 is a reasonable suggestion for future research to confirm direct binding. This is a standard follow-up experiment for transcriptional target identification studies.

results.result: The analysis establishes a GRN regulating cranial sensory organ and neuron development from the PPE, providing an invaluable repository for further functional studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C109 summarize the significance of the study. The establishment of a GRN (C108) is supported by the identification of hundreds of target genes and the functional validation of selected genes. The claim that the data is an invaluable repository (C109) is a reasonable assessment of the study's contribution.

results.result: Cell proliferation, morphogenesis, and cytodifferentiation are affected in human patients with Six1 and Eya1 dysregulation, suggesting that target genes identified in this study may be misregulated in these diseases, potentially opening avenues for therapeutic intervention.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C111 discuss the potential clinical relevance of the findings. The connection to human disease (C110) is supported by citations (Kochhar et al., 2007; Blevins et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016). The speculation about therapeutic intervention (C111) is reasonable but requires further validation.

results.result: The study identified hundreds of novel Six1/Eya1 target genes with potentially important roles for placode development, and loss-of-function studies confirmed that target genes encoding regulators of progenitor fates and neuronal/sensory differentiation require Six1 and Eya1 for their placodal expression, providing pioneering insights into the GRNs regulating placode development.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 and C31-C34 summarize the main findings of the study. The identification of hundreds of novel target genes (C3, C31) is supported by the RNA-Seq data (C39-C44). The loss-of-function validation (C4, C5, C32, C33) is supported by the morpholino and dominant-negative experiments (C73-C75). The claim of pioneering insights (C34) is reasonable given the novelty of the comprehensive screen (C26).
